Record U.S. gas output forces prices lower for longer

U.S. gas production continues to grow as output is boosted by the increasing amounts of associated gas coming from oil wells in the Permian Basin underlying Texas and New Mexico.

Production has accelerated faster than the completion of new liquefied natural gas (LNG) terminals leading to the accumulation of surplus inventories and putting downward pressure on prices.

Production is increasingly a by-product of oil drilling and is becoming more sensitive to the price of crude rather than gas itself — weakening the feedback mechanism within the gas market ...

Hmm. It’s going to be very interesting to watch how this turns out.

Most people familiar with the SPR have long known that Venezuelan heavy crude (and Canadian dilbit) isn’t suitable for the SPR because of quality incompatibility and separation issues.

But that isn’t to say you CANNOT shove this type of crude into the reserves—just that it’s not advisable and will likely cause issues in the future.

Maybe this is less of an issue today given that some of the caverns are now effectively empty (less incompatibility issues with current holdings) or maybe the Trump admin just won’t care about future issues and shove it in there anyway 🤷🏻‍♂️

Based on this Reuters report, sounds like we’ll be finding out sooner than later.

There is precedent for swapping a given set of barrels that the US government has received in-kind for the medium-sour barrels that typically fill the SPR.

But otherwise these will need to be sold off to refineries—and Washington pockets the difference between cost and market $?

Prediction: in 5 years, we’ll see a lot of folks (and most on here) quoting these prices (likely accessible via easy API and without the cost/rules associated with data from the traditional exchanges) rather than the real WTI/Brent contracts explicitly in their charts.

Crude prices turn lower from a five-week high, supporting risk appetite in stocks, while bonds and gold also trade higher. The reversal appears to have been triggered by comments from US Energy Secretary Chris Wright, who said more than 17 million barrels of oil flowed through the Strait of Hormuz on Monday, and that it represented the highest level of crude transit since the Iran war reduced flows. Adding to the more constructive tone, Chinese President Xi Jinping said China is willing to work with Middle Eastern countries to “safeguard” shipping through key regional waterways.

The sharp reversal highlights a market where trader conviction remains low, particularly when it comes to holding long positions, with sentiment and prices liable to turn on a dime in response to any comment suggesting an improvement or deterioration in regional flows.

Fresh figures: Over the past (complete) 28 days, there have been six days where more than 10 million barrels of crude oil departed via the USN Blockade Line.

As you can see, the average daily number is 7.54 Mbpd (down from 17.67 Mbpd back in Jan & Feb 2026).

Of that amount, 5.04 Mbpd comes out via the SoH while another 2.49 Mbpd comes out of the oil terminals located along the GoO.

Crude oil exports via the Strait of Hormuz per our tracking:

- Pre-conflict era (2026-01-01 to 2026-02-28): 16.63 Mbpd
- Pre-US blockade conflict era (2026-02-28 to 2026-04-13): 3.45 Mbpd
- First US blockade (2026-04-13 to 2026-06-18): 2.72 Mbpd
- MoU effective era (2026-06-18 to 2026-07-14): 10 Mbpd
- Second US blockade era (2026-07-14 - present): 4.9 Mbpd

186 days of conflict amounted to 779 million barrels of crude oil via the SoH; which works out to 4.19 Mbpd.
